title_clean: Buying Stocks vs Futures vs Options (Mission Options E11)
summary: Worked comparison of the same SBI position via cash, futures and ITM call options: capital, charges, returns and crash risk. Cash needs full payment, futures one-third margin, options only premium with capped loss.
lessons: Same directional view, three instruments: cash ties up full capital, futures one-third margin, options only premium with loss capped at premium paid.
Short-term directional trades in cash market cost ~10x the charges of futures (~Rs1,684 vs Rs174 on a Rs7.35L position).
Instead of long futures, buy an in-the-money call; instead of short futures, buy an in-the-money put - similar payoff, strictly capped downside.
What matters is return on capital deployed: ~5-6% cash, ~20% futures, ~35% options on the identical Rs45,000 gain.
Stocks can crash 40-70% in a day (DHFL, Infibeam); option buyers' loss stays at premium while cash/futures holders take the full hit.

strategies.name: ITM call instead of long futures
strategies.construction: Buy deep ITM call (e.g. SBI 200CE at Rs46 with spot 245, lot 3000) instead of 1 lot futures
strategies.numbers: Premium ~Rs1.38L vs futures margin ~Rs2.5L vs cash Rs7.35L; at 260: ~Rs45,000 gain all three; charges cash 1,684 / futures 174 / options 329
strategies.best_regime: Strong directional view with defined horizon; want futures-like exposure with capped risk
strategies.adjustments: Exit anytime before expiry; premium tracks underlying
strategies.risks: Max loss = premium paid; decay works against you if the move is delayed past expiry

title_clean: Why NO To Trading E01: 99% Lose Money
summary: Evidence that >99% of traders lose: Zerodha 60-day-challenge winner stats (~1,000 of 1-2 lakh traders), Zerodha CEO's <1% beat-FD claim, Fyers' 90-90-90 rule. Parable: take risk only when life is comfortable.
lessons: Take risk when you are comfortable, not when desperate: lose Rs1-2L from a stable salary and it is two months' income; from unemployment it is ruin.
Ask yourself what makes you the top 1% in a field where 99% fail; without an answer, stay out.
COVID saw over 1 crore new demat accounts - people enter markets hardest exactly when their lives are least stable.
Exceptional winners (like film stars) are exceptions, not the base rate; social media shows you the exceptions.
A college where 99% fail: nobody enrols their child - yet people enrol themselves in trading without asking why they differ.

title_clean: Why NO To Trading E02: Trading Is NOT a Zero-Sum Game
summary: The club-card parable shows the house's cut turns repeated play into structural loss; STT, brokerage, GST and stamp duty drain an estimated Rs50-60,000 crore a year. Even the 1% winners earn only normal returns on margin.
lessons: Trading is a negative-sum game: frictions (STT ~Rs6-8,000 crore/yr; total ~Rs50-60,000 crore) leak out of the system every year.
The 99% losing does not make the 1% rich: a seller earning Rs75,000 on Rs1.5 crore margin makes ~0.5% a month - a normal business return, not a jackpot.
Repeat any game long enough with a house cut and average outcome approaches total loss - the club player lost Rs20-25 lakh over 30 years.
Profit claims without lifestyle or charity proof have a hidden agenda: training, PMS or other monetization of followers.

title_clean: Why NO To Trading E03: The Typical Journey to Failure
summary: The canonical failure arc: buy stagnant stocks, jump to leveraged futures, blow up on an un-hedgeable news gap, chase guru software and 'position sizing' gyan, end up paying trainers from the last 10% of capital. Stocks move 90% in 10% of the time.
lessons: A stock makes 90% of its move in 10% of the time - boredom is the price of holding (Reliance flat 2008-2017, then +400% in 3 years; a power stock flat a decade, then 3x in 3 months).
10x leverage cuts both ways: +1% becomes +10%, but a 5% news gap on 9 lots erases half the capital overnight.
The last-10%-capital recovery mindset is fatal: gamblers who try to win back the final 10% lose that too.
Trainers monetize the desperate: overpriced software (Rs60,000/yr, Rs30,000 commission) and fictitious model portfolios (Rs3L to Rs40L, '2000%') target people who just lost 90%.
Nobody asks why people with big capital should be the stupid ones losing to small accounts - capital wins in every business, including markets.

title_clean: Why NO To Trading E04: Position Sizing and Diversification
summary: Continues the leveraged-trader parable: cutting to 2 lots makes a 10% win worth only 2% of capital - so sizing alone solves nothing. The real answer is diversification across strategies, strikes and timeframes, like splitting money across business, FD, equity, gold and property.
lessons: There is no universal 'right' position size: 9 lots risks ruin, 2 lots makes wins trivial - sizing rules alone do not create returns.
Diversify across strategies, strike prices and timeframes; that is how 80-90% of capital stays deployed without concentrated blow-up risk.
Run capital like a business portfolio: business, FD, equity, gold, property - each leg rescues or funds the others in trouble.
A contrarian in a room of nineteen is either too stupid or too intelligent; only results distinguish them (Thyrocare founder's verdict, 2018).
Believe market advice only from people who have achieved something in the market.

title_clean: Why NO To Trading E05: Stop Loss - A Trader's Worst Enemy
summary: No bank asks a restaurant loan-seeker for a 'stop loss'; businesses diagnose and fix (pricing, sourcing, menu) instead of pre-committing to a 2% shutdown. Mechanical stop-losses die by a thousand cuts in volatile markets; manage positions like a business, not a tripwire.
lessons: Nobody starts a business with a predetermined 'stop loss' - why should a trade, an ownership stake in a business, be any different?
In volatile markets, a stop hits before the move arrives; 1,000 small cuts (many small stops) kill an account as surely as one big loss.
A stop-loss is not a strategy: if it were, the 99% who religiously use stops would be winning.
Not using a stop does not mean riding losses: diagnose like a business owner - is it pricing, costs, or the thesis itself - then fix or exit deliberately.
Rebutting the Mahabharat analogy: the Kauravas' error was gambling at all, not skipping a stop-loss.
quotes: If one cut of a knife can kill a person, a thousand small cuts can also kill.
Position sizing, stop loss, risk management - people talk of many things, but none of them will make you money by themselves.
enhance: Side-by-side: 'tripwire trading' vs 'business diagnosis' decision flow for a losing position

title_clean: How Trainers Mislead You with P&L Reports
summary: Anatomy of fake flexes: a claimed Rs90-lakh year was 20L trading + 70L investment; margin-blocked ledger entries expose sellers posing as buyers. His own mutual fund doubling from the COVID bottom proves 'half-truth' returns. Detection heuristics for influencer P&Ls.
lessons: Margin-blocked ledger lines mean option selling - a 'buyer guru' whose own account shows blocked margin is doing what he does not teach.
Split the claim: trading profit vs investment profit; a 70L investment gain in a bull year (Nifty doubled) is baseline, not skill.
Post-crash +100% years (2009 after Lehman, 2020-21 after COVID) are recoveries, not repeatability - the next decade never repeats them.
Ask the claimant to trade YOUR money for a profit share; real performers accept, screenshot-flexers refuse.
If a 90L/yr claimant has 30Cr net worth, why flex daily for 20L instead of scaling capital? The incentive reveals the truth.

title_clean: My 15-Year Journey: Advice on Capital, Patience and Trust
summary: Life-phase framework: work for money till ~40, then let money work for you; accumulate first, trade second. With small capital, skip F&O and use IPOs (sell partially, keep free shares). 'Less is more': consistent 20-30% plus trust beats gambling flexes.
lessons: Two life phases: until ~40 you work for money; after that money must work for you - trade only accumulated capital, not salary-sized bets.
Small capital belongs in quality IPOs, not F&O: get allotment, sell part to recover cost, hold the rest as free shares - one may multi-bag.
Less is more: 10L at 100% is 10L/yr; 20-30% compounded consistently attracts other people's money, which is how fortunes actually scale.
Trust is the real leverage: people with money distrust MTM flexers and back consistent, transparent performers.
Recognition takes years of patience - visibility (conferences, media) came long after skill.

strategies.name: IPO cost-recovery hold
strategies.construction: Apply to quality IPOs with idle funds parked in 6-6.5% savings accounts; on allotment sell partial quantity to recover application cost; hold remainder free
strategies.numbers: Example: L&T issue ~1987-88, partly convertible debentures Rs50 doubled to ~Rs100 next day; held value estimated Rs50-60L today
strategies.best_regime: Small capital, no F&O skill yet; strong primary-market pipelines
strategies.adjustments: Review holdings annually; keep proceeds cycling into fresh quality IPOs
strategies.risks: Opportunity cost if markets run; allotment not guaranteed (refund is safe)

title_clean: Hedge Funds vs Mutual Funds vs PMS
summary: India's managed-money menu: MFs (any amount, cash-only, 1:1 hedging, now covered calls on Nifty-50 stocks), PMS (Rs50L min, 2%+20%, micro-caps), AIF Cat-III (Rs1Cr min, F&O allowed, rare). Hedge defined honestly: a compound wall, not a bunker - and insurance you buy at entry, not after a 50% fall.
lessons: A hedge is a compound wall, not a bunker: it converts unlimited loss into limited loss; 100% hedging produces 0% return.
Buy insurance when you buy the car: hedge at position open, never after the share has already fallen 50%.
Vehicle fees shape risk-taking: MFs (1-1.5%) stay plain; PMS (2% + 20%) chase micro-caps; only AIF Cat-III may use F&O - and few exist.
Mutual funds may hedge 1:1 (short futures equal to holdings) and recently sell covered calls on Nifty-50 stocks only.
If you hold shares and sell calls against them, upside beyond the strike is capped - know what each structure gives up.

strategies.name: Protective put (vehicle-insurance hedge)
strategies.construction: Long shares (e.g. Reliance at 2,000) + buy 1,900 put
strategies.numbers: Max loss ~Rs100/share plus premium instead of Rs1,000 in a black-swan fall to 1,000
strategies.best_regime: Any long equity position opened with event/earnings risk ahead
strategies.adjustments: Roll the put on rallies; ladder strikes for cheaper protection
strategies.risks: Premium drag; protection only while held

summary: Debt-instrument tour: FDs post-tax 2-3%, debt MFs carry default pass-through (DHFL, IL&FS), plain bonds can go to zero (Yes Bank, Lakshmi Vilas). Covered bonds add dual recourse via trustee-held collateral; a retail platform opened them from Rs10,000 at ~10.25%.
lessons: Judge any debt instrument on SLR - Safety, Liquidity, Return - in that order, never return alone.
Covered bonds give dual recourse: the issuer's promise plus trustee-held collateral (gold, housing loans, vehicle pools), so default does not mean zero.
Plain bondholders can be wiped to zero in resolution (Yes Bank, Lakshmi Vilas Bank) while equity sometimes recovers half - unsecured debt is not 'safe'.
Debt mutual funds pass corporate defaults straight to investors; DHFL and IL&FS shocks left several debt funds below FD returns.
In a 4-5% FD world, 10%+ with collateral cover is attractive even post-tax (~7% in the 30% slab).

strategies.construction: Via retail covered-bond platform: minimum ~Rs10,000; pools collateralized by vehicle/gold/housing loan books held by a trustee
strategies.numbers: Issue cited: 10.25% p.a., monthly payouts, ~23-month maturity, ~Rs20 crore pool; historical HNI entry was Rs10 lakh minimum
strategies.best_regime: Low-rate environment; investors wanting FD-beating yield with collateral protection
strategies.adjustments: Ladder maturities across issues; prefer diverse collateral pools
strategies.risks: Secondary liquidity not guaranteed - be able to hold full term; platform/issuer concentration
